Repair
rē-pâr´
v. (to restore what is broken or decayed; rendering Hebrew chazaq, banah, Greek anoikodomeo)
From Latin reparo, to make ready again. Scripture's repairs are of altars, walls, and houses of God — and the man who does them is given one of the most honourable titles in the prophets.

Biblical Definition

To repair is to restore what has fallen into ruin, and Scripture treats the work as honourable rather than merely remedial. Isaiah gives the repairer a name: “thou shalt be called, The repairer of the breach, The restorer of paths to dwell in” (Isaiah 58:12). The title is conferred in a chapter about true fasting, so that repairing is presented as the fruit of real religion rather than as a substitute for it. Kings are commended for the same instinct toward the house of God: “it came to pass after this, that Joash was minded to repair the house of the LORD” (2 Chronicles 24:4). The mindedness comes first and the masonry follows. The most charged repair in Scripture is Elijah's on Carmel, performed in front of a nation that had abandoned the altar it belonged to: “And Elijah said unto all the people, Come near unto me. And all the people came near unto him. And he repaired the altar of the LORD that was broken down” (1 Kings 18:30). Before fire fell, an old altar was rebuilt. Nehemiah supplies the working principle for every such labour, and it is not chiefly technique: “So built we the wall; and all the wall was joined together unto the half thereof: for the people had a mind to work” (Nehemiah 4:6).

Webster 1828 Definition

To restore to a sound state what is decayed, dilapidated or injured; to mend; to make good again. Scripture honours the repairer of the breach, records kings minded to repair God's house, and sets Elijah repairing a broken altar before fire fell.

expand to see more

REPAIR, v.t. [L. reparo; re and paro, to prepare.] To restore to a sound or good state after decay, injury, dilapidation or partial destruction; as, to repair a house or a wall.

2. To rebuild a part decayed or destroyed; to make amends by an equivalent.

3. To fill up again; to restore; as, to repair a loss or waste.

REPAIR, v.i. To go to; to betake oneself; to resort; as, to repair to a city.

REPAIR, n. Restoration to a sound state; supply of loss; reparation; also, state as regards repairing.

REPAIRER, n. One who repairs, restores or makes amends.

Key Scripture

Isaiah 58:12 — "And they that shall be of thee shall build the old waste places: thou shalt raise up the foundations of many generations; and thou shalt be called, The repairer of the breach, The restorer of paths to dwell in."

2 Chronicles 24:4 — "And it came to pass after this, that Joash was minded to repair the house of the LORD."

1 Kings 18:30 — "And Elijah said unto all the people, Come near unto me. And all the people came near unto him. And he repaired the altar of the LORD that was broken down."

Nehemiah 4:6 — "So built we the wall; and all the wall was joined together unto the half thereof: for the people had a mind to work."

Modern Corruption

Repair has fallen out of favour as a category: what is broken is replaced, rebranded, or abandoned, and a church in decay is more readily left for a new one than mended by the men who belong to it.

expand to see more

Elijah's act on Carmel is easy to read past. Before the contest, before the fire, he repaired the altar of the LORD that was broken down — an old altar, on an old foundation, in the pattern God had given. He did not erect a novel one better suited to the moment. Reformation in Scripture consistently takes that shape: not the invention of something unprecedented, but the rebuilding of what was there and had been let fall. Where a generation assumes that faithfulness requires starting fresh, it loses the very thing Isaiah 58:12 promises to honour, since a breach can only be repaired by someone willing to work on a wall he did not build.

The opposite error treats repair as a matter of masonry alone. Joash was minded to repair the house of the LORD, and Nehemiah's wall rose because the people had a mind to work; in both cases the disposition is named as the cause. Buildings, budgets, and programmes can be restored while the thing they exist to house is neglected, and Joash's own later history is the warning — the man who repaired the temple ended by forsaking the God whose house it was. Repair that stops at the fabric is not what the prophet was commending.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chazaq (to strengthen, to repair) is the recurring verb of Nehemiah's wall; banah (to build) and rapha (to heal, mend) fill out the field, with Greek anoikodomeo (to build again) in the New Testament.

expand to see more

Hebrew chazaq (H2388) — to be strong, to strengthen, to repair; the verb repeated through Nehemiah 3 of each man repairing his portion.

Hebrew banah (H1129) — to build; used of building the old waste places in Isaiah 58:12.

Hebrew rapha (H7495) — to heal, to mend; used of Elijah repairing the broken altar in 1 Kings 18:30.

Hebrew perets (H6556) — a breach, a gap; the thing the honoured repairer closes.

Greek anoikodomeo (G456) — to build again, to rebuild; used of raising up the fallen tabernacle of David in Acts 15.

Usage

"“The repairer of the breach” — mending a wall one did not build is given an honourable name."

"“He repaired the altar of the LORD that was broken down” — reformation rebuilds the old pattern."

"“The people had a mind to work” — the disposition is named as the cause of the building."
